title: 40 Solo Founder and Solopreneur Statistics That Reveal the Future of One-Person Businesses
summary: Comprehensive market data showing why solo entrepreneurs are reshaping the startup landscape and how AI-powered tools are accelerating their success…
body_markdown:
*Comprehensive market data showing why solo entrepreneurs are reshaping the startup landscape and how AI-powered tools are accelerating their success*


According to Carta, the share of new startups with solo founders[rose from 23.7% to 36.3%](https://carta.com/data/solo-founders-report/) between 2019 and H1 2025, highlighting the growing role of solo founders in entrepreneurship. Yet despite this growth, solo founders face persistent challenges: limited technical resources, time constraints, and the burden of wearing every hat simultaneously. Modern[AI app builders](https://floot.com/blog/ai-app-builders-backend-platforms) are changing this equation, helping solopreneurs create working applications through natural-language instructions while still requiring testing before launch.


## **Key Takeaways**


- **Solo founding has surged significantly.** Between 2019 and H1 2025, the share of new startups with solo founders increased by about 53%.[AI app builders](https://floot.com/blog/best-ai-app-builders-for-non-technical-founders-in-2026) can help non-technical founders develop applications without setting up every service themselves.
- **First-year profitability is possible with lean operations.** In Gusto's survey of businesses started in 2024, 77% of responding solopreneurs reported first-year profitability.[MVP development tools](https://floot.com/blog/ai-app-builders-mvp-development) can help founders test software ideas without hiring an entire development team.
- **Startup funding often comes from founders.** Nearly half of new solopreneur businesses in Gusto's 2024 sample started with less than $5,000, and 84% of those needing financing used personal funds. Floot is[free to start](https://floot.com/en/pricing) , with usage limits and hosting allowances.
- **GenAI is already helping with business tasks.** Among surveyed GenAI-using solopreneurs, 64 percent used it for marketing. Floot's[MCP connector](https://floot.com/docs) allows supported assistants to handle app development while Floot manages infrastructure.
- **Building an app does not require building its infrastructure.**[Floot's full-stack platform](https://floot.com/blog/ai-app-builders-backend-platforms) provides managed hosting, PostgreSQL, authentication, storage, and publishing workflows for founders who need apps with saved data.


## **The Rise of the Solopreneur: Key Statistics and Trends**


The solopreneur economy represents a fundamental shift in how businesses form and operate. From 2012 to 2023, the number of U.S. nonemployer establishments grew an average[2.7% annually](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/07/nonemployer-business-growth.html) , compared with 1.1% for employer establishments.


### **1. Nearly 32 million U.S. nonemployer establishments were recorded in 2024**


The U.S. Census Bureau recorded[31,985,874 nonemployer establishments](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/) in 2024. This measure counts business establishments rather than unique solopreneurs, and it includes businesses operating under different legal forms. Nonemployer statistics describe firms without paid employees, not necessarily founders who intend to work alone permanently. The figure provides a broad measure of owner-operated business activity across the economy.


### **2. 82.3% of small businesses have no employees**


According to the SBA's February 2026 report,[82.3 percent](https://www.nyssbdc.org/resources/smallbizstats.html) of U.S. small businesses had no employees, based on 2022 business counts. That equals approximately 29.8 million nonemployer firms in the report's dataset. It highlights how widespread businesses without payroll employees are, although not all such firms identify as solopreneur ventures or intend to remain owner-only.


### **3. Solo founder share rose 53% in six years**


The share of new startups with solo founders[rose from 23.7% to 36.3%](https://carta.com/data/solo-founders-report/) between 2019 and H1 2025. That represents roughly a[53% relative increase](https://solofounders.com/report) in the solo-founded share, not a 53-percentage-point gain. Carta's figures describe startups in its dataset rather than all U.S. business formations. The trend nevertheless shows a growing presence of single-founder companies in that market.


### **4. 56% of surveyed solopreneurs started after 2020**


An Intuit QuickBooks survey found that[56% of responding](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/r/small-business-data/self-employment-trends-2024/) solopreneurs started their businesses after 2020. The survey examined self-employment trends in 2024 and reflects the experiences of its respondents rather than every solo business owner. The result suggests that a substantial share of surveyed entrepreneurs launched recently, amid changing attitudes toward work, income, and independence.


## **Understanding the Solopreneur: Defining the Solo Business Owner**


Solopreneurs differ from traditional entrepreneurs in their approach to growth and team building. They prioritize autonomy, flexibility, and direct control over their business operations.


### **5. 53% of surveyed solopreneurs started driven by passion**


In Simply Business's 2025 survey of solopreneur customers,[53% cited pursuing](https://www.simplybusiness.com/resource/2025-solopreneur-report/) a passion as a motivation for starting their business. The report also identified autonomy and supplemental income as other common reasons. These findings describe why people in the survey began working independently, but they do not establish that passion alone improves survival rates or guarantees business success.


### **6. 41% rely on their business as primary income**


In the same Simply Business survey,[41% of respondents](https://www.simplybusiness.com/resource/2025-solopreneur-report/) said their business was their primary income source and that they operated it full-time. Other respondents ran their ventures alongside another job or additional sources of income. This distinction matters because not every business without employees represents a person's sole occupation, even when the owner manages its operations independently.


### **7. 42% of solopreneurs are aged 35-54**


According to Gusto's analysis,[42% of solopreneurs](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/solopreneurship-viability) were aged 35-54 in its 2023 data, with ages 35-44 forming the largest single group. This shows that owner-only work is not limited to founders just entering the workforce. The findings describe a substantial presence of experienced professionals using their skills and contacts to operate independently.


### **8. Women owned 42.7% of nonemployer businesses in 2022**


Women owned[42.7% of U.S.](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/05/small-business-week.html) nonemployer businesses in 2022, according to Census Bureau data. That represented about 12.7 million businesses without paid employees. The statistic reflects participation in the broader nonemployer economy, including different industries and business structures. It should not be interpreted as the percentage of venture-backed startups founded by women.


## **Starting Lean: Statistics on Small Business Launch Costs and Funding**


Solopreneurs consistently demonstrate an ability to launch with minimal capital, relying on personal resources and lean operational approaches. Tools such as[Floot's app-building platform](https://floot.com/en/pricing) are free to start and let founders work through supported AI assistants while Floot provides managed app infrastructure.


### **9. 84% of solopreneurs seeking startup financing used personal funds**


Among new solopreneurs who needed startup financing in 2024,[84% used personal funds](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) to launch their businesses, according to Gusto's survey. This reliance on the founders' own money reduces dependence on external backers, although it can expose personal savings to business risk. The figure applies only to surveyed solopreneurs who sought startup financing, not to every new business.


### **10. Almost half started with less than $5,000**


Nearly half of solopreneur businesses launched in 2024 started with less than[$5,000 in capital](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) in Gusto's survey. This compares with only 10% of employer businesses in the same research. Starting without employees can reduce initial payroll commitments, although other expenses still depend on industry, equipment, licensing, and the services a business needs.


### **11. Solo founders received 14.7% of cash raised in priced equity rounds**


Although solo-led companies represented 30% of startups founded in Carta's 2024 cohort, they received just[14.7% of cash raised](https://carta.com/data/solo-founders-report/) in priced equity rounds that year. The figures describe different aspects of Carta's startup population: company formations and venture dollars. They indicate a funding disparity without proving that any individual solo founder is unable to raise capital.


### **12. Solo founders represented 17% of startups that closed VC rounds**


Solo founders represented 35% of companies incorporated on Carta in 2024, but accounted for only[17% of companies](https://carta.com/data/founder-ownership/) from that cohort that closed a venture capital round before year-end. This comparison concerns the same incorporation-year cohort. It indicates a difference in early fundraising outcomes, not necessarily the longer-term prospects of every solo-founded company.


## **Solo Founder Equity and Fundraising Patterns**


Fundraising and equity ownership differ between solo-founded startups and companies with multiple founders. These statistics describe founding-team ownership and venture capital financing rather than the legal differences between sole proprietorships and LLCs.


### **13. 80% of companies that raised capital had multiple founders**


According to Carta,[80% of companies](https://carta.com/data/win-over-pre-seed-investors/) that successfully raised capital across funding stages in 2025 had multiple founders. Two-founder teams were the most common among these funded companies. This describes the composition of fundraising companies rather than a requirement imposed on entrepreneurs, and it does not mean that solo-founded startups are ineligible for venture investment.


### **14. 45.9% of two-founder teams split equity equally**


Among two-founder teams on Carta,[45.9% divided founder equity](https://carta.com/data/founder-ownership/) equally in 2024, up from 31.5% in 2015. The increase shows that equal splits have become more frequent among teams with two founders. Solo founders do not face a co-founder split at formation, although outside investment, employee equity, and later financing can still reduce their ownership.


### **15. Median founding team ownership drops to 23% after Series B**


Carta reported that the median founding team collectively owned[56.2% after seed funding](https://carta.com/data/founder-ownership/) , 36.1% after Series A, and 23% after Series B. These percentages refer to the founding team's combined stake, not the portion held by any one founder. The figures illustrate dilution as companies raise successive rounds and issue equity to investors.


## **Nonemployer Businesses by Industry**


Nonemployer businesses are present across a wide range of sectors. Professional services lead in establishment counts, while real estate leads in total nonemployer receipts in the cited Census Bureau data.


### **16. Professional services lead with 4 million establishments**


In 2022, Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services accounted for[4,013,209 nonemployer establishments](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/05/smallest-businesses.html) , representing 13.5% of U.S. nonemployer businesses. This category includes varied forms of professional and technical work, not only software businesses. It was the largest sector by nonemployer establishment count in the cited Census data, illustrating the breadth of independent service activity.


### **17. Real estate nonemployers generated $344.7 billion in 2022**


In 2022, Real Estate, Rental and Leasing generated[$344.7 billion](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/05/smallest-businesses.html) in nonemployer business receipts, representing 20% of total nonemployer receipts that year. Receipts measure business activity rather than an owner's take-home income or profit. The sector generated the largest total in the Census Bureau's 2022 nonemployer breakdown, despite accounting for a smaller share of establishments.


### **18. Tech solopreneurs in Gusto's sample exceed $700,000 by year five**


Gusto's five-year revenue findings cover businesses that remained active for at least five years on its platform, not all U.S. solopreneurs. Information-sector solopreneurs, including software developers and tech consultants, averaged more than 50% annual revenue growth and exceeded[$700,000 in revenue](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/solopreneurship-viability) by year five. These results describe a specific surviving-business sample rather than typical earnings for every new technology venture.


## **Scaling Solo: Growth Strategies for One-Person Businesses**


Solo founders can expand capacity through employees, contractors, and automation without beginning with a large founding team. The following results distinguish hiring patterns from the adoption of AI for everyday work.


### **19. Solo founders hire first employee in 399 days**


Solo founders bring on their first employee after a median of[399 days from incorporation](https://carta.com/data/solo-founders-report/) , compared with 480 days for multi-founder companies, according to Carta. These are medians among the companies included in the analysis, not deadlines or recommended hiring schedules. The figures suggest that some solo-founded startups begin hiring sooner even though their initial founding teams are smaller.


### **20. 34% of new solopreneurs hired contractors in their first year**


According to Gusto,[34% of new solopreneurs](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) surveyed about businesses started in 2024 hired at least one contractor in their first year. Contractors can add capacity without becoming permanent payroll employees. This helps explain why an enterprise can be classified as a nonemployer while still paying other people for specific projects or ongoing services.


### **21. 64% of GenAI-using solopreneurs use it for marketing**


In Gusto's survey of new businesses,[64 percent](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) of GenAI-using solopreneurs reported using the technology to assist with marketing. The percentage concerns solopreneurs who already used generative AI, not all solopreneurs in the study. Marketing tasks may include generating and revising materials, but the survey figure alone does not measure the effectiveness of those activities.


### **22. 52% of personal-services GenAI users use it for customer service**


In Gusto's survey,[52 percent](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) of GenAI-using solopreneurs in personal services used it for customer service tasks. The industry-specific denominator matters because these respondents already used GenAI. Automating or assisting with customer communications may save time, but founders still need to review responses and handle cases that require human attention.


### **23. 36% of GenAI users apply it to sales**


In the same Gusto survey,[36 percent](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) of GenAI-using solopreneurs reported applying it to sales-related tasks. These activities can include preparing outreach materials and organizing follow-up work, depending on the business. The statistic measures reported use, not higher conversion rates or additional revenue generated by AI-assisted sales processes.


## **Solopreneur Profitability and Revenue Growth**


Gusto's research describes first-year profitability among surveyed businesses that started in 2024 and revenue growth among a separate sample of longer-lived businesses. These findings describe different groups rather than guaranteed outcomes for all solopreneurs.


### **24. 77% of surveyed 2024 solopreneurs reported first-year profitability**


In Gusto's survey of solopreneurs who started businesses in 2024,[77% reported being profitable](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) in their first year. This was higher than the 54% reported by employer businesses in the same survey. The finding is self-reported and survey-specific, so it should not be treated as the profitability rate of every new U.S. owner-only business.


### **25. Average first-year revenue was $294,000 in Gusto's sample**


Gusto's longer-term analysis found average business[revenue of about $294,000](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/solopreneurship-viability) in the first year. Revenue is not the same as owner pay, profit, or disposable income. The sample consists of businesses that remained active for at least five years on Gusto's platform, so it does not represent the full range of outcomes among newly launched solopreneur ventures.


### **26. Revenue exceeds $500,000 by year five in Gusto's sample**


By their fifth year, solopreneurs in Gusto's longer-lived-business sample averaged[over $500,000](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/solopreneurship-viability) in annual revenue. The increase is consistent with the report's findings on business growth over time. It is important to distinguish this average among surviving businesses from a forecast for a newly started venture, which may earn less, remain smaller, or close earlier.


### **27. Millennial solopreneurs in Gusto's sample see 25% annual growth**


Gusto reported that millennial solopreneurs in its longer-lived-business[sample averaged 25%](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/solopreneurship-viability) annual revenue growth and reached about $525,000 in average revenue by year five. These figures apply to the age cohort within the study, not to all millennial business owners. They also describe business revenue rather than personal earnings retained after expenses and taxes.


## **Overcoming Challenges: Common Hurdles for Solo Founders**


Despite their advantages, solopreneurs face distinct challenges around time management, uncertain income, stress, and handling every business function. Understanding these obstacles helps solo builders prepare more realistically.


### **28. 41% cite time management as a major challenge**


In Gusto's survey,[Forty-one percent](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) of new solopreneurs identified time management as a major operational challenge. The difficulty was reported across multiple industries, including professional services. Founders working alone often need to divide their time between client work, administration, and business development. The statistic measures a reported challenge rather than hours worked or productivity lost.


### **29. 48% of surveyed solopreneurs have gone at least a month without income**


In Simply Business's 2025 survey,[48% of responding solopreneurs](https://www.simplybusiness.com/resource/2025-solopreneur-report/) reported going at least a month without income. This illustrates why cash reserves and predictable billing can matter even to an owner who has a steady flow of work at other times. The finding comes from the insurer's surveyed customers, so it should not be generalized to all independent business owners.


### **30. 35% report high stress levels**


In Intuit QuickBooks' 2024 research,[35% of surveyed solopreneurs](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/r/small-business-data/self-employment-trends-2024/) rated their stress as high, compared with 26% of surveyed business owners who had employees. The results suggest that independence does not eliminate pressure from business operations. These are self-reported perceptions among survey respondents, not clinical assessments or population-wide mental health estimates.


### **31. 61% underestimated handling every business function**


Simply Business reported that[61% of surveyed solopreneurs](https://www.simplybusiness.com/resource/2025-solopreneur-report/) underestimated the challenge of managing all business functions independently. Working alone can mean combining sales, finance, service delivery, and administration within one role. The finding points to the importance of realistic workload planning, although it does not establish which particular tools or practices would improve outcomes for all respondents.


### **32. 34% have considered giving up**


In the Simply Business survey,[34% of respondents](https://www.simplybusiness.com/resource/2025-solopreneur-report/) said they had considered giving up their business. Among that group, 72% identified financial stress or inconsistent income as a reason. The second percentage applies to people who had considered quitting, not the entire survey. Both figures highlight pressures experienced by the respondents without predicting whether they will actually close their businesses.


## **Tech for Solopreneurs: Essential Tools and Platforms**


AI assistants, application platforms, and automation can help solo founders cover business functions that once required more specialized support. The following figures concern how surveyed solopreneurs used generative AI.


### **33. 47% of GenAI-using solopreneurs use it to save time**


Among GenAI-using solopreneurs in Gusto's survey,[47% said they used](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) it to reduce time spent on tedious tasks. The comparable figure among employer business owners using GenAI was 37%. These are reported reasons for using the technology rather than measured reductions in work hours, but they help explain why task automation attracts solo operators.


### **34. 75 percent of GenAI-using professional-services solopreneurs use it for marketing**


Gusto's research found that[75 percent](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) of GenAI-using professional-services solopreneurs applied it to marketing. This was higher than the overall 64 percent share among GenAI-using solopreneurs in the same survey. The comparison suggests differences in how sectors use the technology, but it does not measure marketing campaign results or customer acquisition improvements.


### **35. 22 percent of GenAI-using solopreneurs use it for legal tasks**


Gusto's survey found that[22 percent](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/new-business-formation-solopreneurs-2025) of GenAI-using solopreneurs used it to assist with legal tasks. The figure captures reported use of AI, not the accuracy or reliability of its legal output. Business owners still need to check relevant legal requirements and obtain qualified professional advice when a task involves contracts, compliance, or material liability.


## **The Future of Solo: Ownership and Growth Trends**


The solo founder trend is reflected in differences in equity ownership, fundraising timelines, and the outcomes of established owner-only businesses. These comparisons describe particular datasets and should not be read as guarantees.


### **36. Solo founders retain 75% more ownership at exit**


Between 2019 and H1 2025, median ownership at exit was[75% greater for solo founders](https://solofounders.com/report) than for lead founders in multi-founder companies, according to a report drawing on Carta data. The comparison concerns personal equity stakes, not the size of exit proceeds. A larger ownership percentage does not necessarily mean a higher financial payout if company valuations differ.


### **37. Solo-founded companies raised first priced rounds sooner in 2018–2024 cohorts**


Solo-founded companies raised their first priced equity rounds sooner than companies with co-founders in every cohort year from[2018–2024](https://solofounders.com/report) , according to the report. This describes the observed timing of priced rounds among the compared startups, not a promise that any single founder will raise funding quickly. The same report notes that overall time to first priced round has been increasing.


### **38. Gusto's sampled solopreneurs averaged 15% annual revenue growth**


Solopreneurs in Gusto's longer-lived-business analysis averaged a[15% annual revenue](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/solopreneurship-viability) increase across their first five years, with certain sectors growing faster. This is an average for businesses that remained active long enough to enter the analysis. It should not be interpreted as a typical return available to every person who launches an owner-only business.


### **39. Average owner pay in Gusto's sample exceeds $87,000 by year five**


Gusto's analysis found that average solopreneur gross pay was about $41,000 in year one, rose to roughly $76,000 in year two, and rose to[more than $87,000](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/solopreneurship-viability) by year five. These are earnings figures for the report's longer-lived businesses, rather than revenue or after-tax take-home pay. They also differ substantially from the business revenue figures in the same study.


### **40. Sampled solopreneurs earn 25% more by year five than comparable employees**


In Gusto's analysis, solopreneurs who remained active for at least five years earned about[25% more in gross pay](https://gusto.com/resources/gusto-insights/solopreneurship-viability) by year five than similarly skilled employees. The comparison accounts for factors described in the report and is specific to its study population. It does not guarantee that solo entrepreneurship will outperform employment for any individual founder.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


These answers clarify the business models, risks, and technology considerations behind the statistics.


### **What is the primary difference between a solopreneur and a small business owner?**


A solopreneur intentionally operates without employees, often as a strategic choice to maintain control and flexibility. Small business owners may employ staff and pursue traditional growth. While the SBA reported that 82.3 percent of small businesses had no employees in its 2022 data, not all owners of those businesses identify as solopreneurs or intend to remain owner-only.


### **What are the most common challenges faced by solo founders?**


Time management was cited by 41% of new solopreneurs in Gusto's survey. Separate research found that 61% of Simply Business respondents underestimated handling every function themselves and 48% had gone at least a month without income. Founders can explore[internal tools development](https://floot.com/blog/ai-app-builders-internal-tools) to organize recurring tasks, while still budgeting for cash flow and customer acquisition.


### **How can a solopreneur protect their personal assets and choose the right business structure?**


Business structure selection is important. Sole proprietorships are generally simple to establish but do not create a separate legal liability shield. LLCs and corporations can provide limited liability protection, subject to applicable law, while S-corp status generally concerns federal tax treatment. The appropriate structure depends on risk, jurisdiction, taxes, and business plans, so professional advice may be worthwhile.


### **What types of businesses are best suited for solopreneurs?**


Professional and technical services represented 4,013,209 nonemployer establishments in the 2022 Census data, while real estate generated the highest nonemployer receipts at $344.7 billion. These are industry totals rather than individual success rates. Digital products and service workflows can also be tested as[MVP applications](https://floot.com/blog/ai-app-builders-mvp-development) , with the required features depending on customers and operational needs.


### **Can a non-technical solopreneur build and launch a professional app?**


Yes. A founder can use Floot with supported AI assistants to create, edit, test, and publish working applications while Floot manages the database, hosting, authentication, and other infrastructure. The specific actions available depend on connector permissions, and launch readiness still requires testing. See[Floot pricing](https://floot.com/en/pricing) for current plan limits, hosting allowances, and mobile requirements; app-store distribution is not automatic.
